# What Gemini Can Do for Your Resume, and How to Approach Your Rough Notes

> **In short:** Google says Gemini, its AI assistant, can turn raw notes about your work into resume bullet points that are clear and ATS-friendly (easy for resume-scanning software to read). Google describes this as a four-step process. The steps themselves are not in the announcement we are working from, so this guide covers the general idea.

You have probably done great work that never made it onto your resume. Your notes from a project might be a messy list of half-sentences, and turning them into something a hiring manager will read is harder than it sounds. That is where Gemini may help.

## What Google says Gemini can do

According to Google's announcement, Gemini can take rough notes and shape them into resume bullets. A bullet is one line on your resume that describes a single achievement or responsibility. Google also says the result is designed to be ATS-friendly.

An ATS (applicant tracking system) is software many employers use to collect and scan applications before a person reads them. Some of these systems look for familiar job terms and simple formatting, so a clear, plain bullet is usually easier for them to read than a fancy one.

Google presents the process as four steps for polishing your professional profile. We do not have those four steps in the material we are working from, so we will not invent them here.

## The general idea behind it

Whatever the exact steps are, the approach is simple to picture:

- **Start with your raw notes.** Write down what you did, even if it is messy. Examples: "helped the team move to new software" or "handled customer complaints, fixed billing errors."
- **Ask the AI to shape them.** A prompt (the instruction you type to an AI) tells it what to do. For example: "Turn these notes into three resume bullets for a customer service role. Start each with an action verb and keep each under two lines."
- **Check the result against what really happened.** AI can sometimes make things sound bigger than they were, or add details you never gave it. Only keep claims you can back up in an interview.

## A few things to watch for

- **Numbers.** If you know a real figure, such as the number of customers you helped, add it. If you don't, don't guess.
- **Job-specific words.** Look at the job posting and see which words it uses. If your experience matches those words, you can use them too.
- **Your voice.** The bullets should still sound like you could explain them out loud.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life**: If you are changing jobs or asking for a raise, you can use an AI assistant to get your past work into a clear written form before you update your resume.
- **For your business or work**: If you manage a team, you can use this approach to help colleagues describe their own work for performance reviews, as long as you check the wording.
- **If you're just getting started**: Begin with one job you had. Write five rough notes about it, then ask Gemini to turn them into three bullets. Compare the result with your own memory of the work.
- **If you already use it**: Try giving Gemini a job posting along with your notes, and ask it to point out where your experience lines up with the posting's wording. Then rewrite anything that sounds too general.

## Wrap-up

Gemini, according to Google, can help turn rough work notes into clear, ATS-friendly resume bullets. The idea is straightforward: give it honest notes, ask for a clear rewrite, and check every claim before you use it. Today, pick one recent project, write down five messy notes about it, and see what a clear bullet looks like.
